question.stem: Doubling the IV bolus dose of a drug that follows linear, first-order pharmacokinetics results in a 2-fold increase in the duration of activity.

options.why: Choosing this treats duration as proportional to dose. The dose sits inside a logarithm, teff = 1.44 t½ ln({{frac:D0|VD × Ceff}}), so doubling it adds ln 2 over k, one half-life, to teff instead of doubling it.

Doubling D0 doubles C0, and the level needs exactly one half-life to fall from 2C0 back to C0; after that it follows the old curve. teff grows by one t½: 26.35 hr becomes 30.97 hr when 250 mg is doubled to 500 mg (VD 24 L, k 0.15 hr⁻¹).

list: teff: the time one IV bolus keeps the plasma level at or above Ceff, the minimum effective concentration.
From C = C0e^(−kt) with C = Ceff: teff = {{frac:ln C0 − ln Ceff|k}}, where C0 = {{frac:D0|VD}}, the level just after the bolus.
With k = {{frac:0.693|t½}}: teff = 1.44 t½ ln({{frac:D0|VD × Ceff}}); 1.44 is {{frac:1|0.693}}.
The dose is inside the logarithm, so doubling it adds {{frac:ln 2|k}}, one half-life, to teff; it does not double teff.
Built for a single IV bolus, a one-compartment open model and first-order elimination.

question.stem: Drugs that display Michaelis-Menten saturation kinetics will often exhibit zero-order kinetics at low concentrations and first-order kinetics at high concentrations.

options.why: Choosing this reverses the two ends. Well below KM the rate is {{frac:Vmax|KM}} × Cp, proportional to concentration, which is first order; well above KM the rate equals Vmax whatever the concentration, which is zero order.

The statement has the orders the other way round. At low concentrations, Cp much less than KM, elimination looks first order; at high concentrations, Cp much greater than KM, the enzyme runs at Vmax and elimination looks zero order.

list: −{{frac:dCp|dt}} = {{frac:Vmax × Cp|KM + Cp}} (Michaelis-Menten kinetics).
Cp much greater than KM: KM is negligible, the rate equals Vmax and does not depend on concentration, which is zero order.
Cp much less than KM: the rate is {{frac:Vmax|KM}} × Cp = k′Cp, proportional to concentration, which is first order.

question.stem: The trapezoidal rule provides a simple way to estimate the AUC.

options.why: The trapezoidal rule breaks the curve into segments between the measured points, finds the area of each, one half base times height summed over the two sides, and adds them. It estimates the AUC from the data alone.

Picking this reads the existence of other routes as ruling the rule out. AUC can also be calculated from the dose and the clearance, AUC = {{frac:D0|Cl}}, but the trapezoidal rule remains a way to estimate it from measured points.

list: AUC tells the extent of drug available for the body to use: the extent of drug absorbed.
Trapezoidal rule, one segment: AUC = ({{frac:Cn−1 + Cn|2}})(tn − tn−1); the segments are summed.
Without data points, AUC = {{frac:D0|Cl}} for an IV dose, and {{frac:FD0|Cl}} for an oral one.

question.stem: The rate of a first-order process is independent of the concentration of drug present.

options.why: Picking True reads "independent" as a first-order property. In a first-order process the rate is k times the concentration, dC/dt = −kC, so the rate is fastest where there is most drug and slows as the drug is eliminated. A rate independent of concentration is zero order, dC/dt = −k.

The first-order rate depends on the concentration present: dC/dt = −kC. On the curve the slope is steepest at the start, where there is most drug, and flattens as the drug is eliminated. What is independent of concentration in first order is the half-life, {{frac:0.693|k}}.

teach.h: Rate and half-life in the two orders
list: First order: the rate depends on the concentration, {{frac:dC|dt}} = −kC; the half-life does not, t½ = {{frac:0.693|k}}.
Zero order: the rate is independent of the concentration, {{frac:dC|dt}} = −k; the half-life depends on it, t½ = {{frac:C0|2k}}.
Read which quantity the statement names, the rate or the half-life, before answering.

question.quote: If we're thinking about the rate being the slope, higher, steeper slope up here where we've got more drug in the body ... so the rate depends on the concentration that's there

question.stem: The half-life of a first-order process is independent of the concentration of drug present.

options.why: First-order half-life is t½ = {{frac:0.693|k}}: a constant divided by a constant. No concentration appears in it, so the time to fall from 100 to 50 mg/L is the same as from 10 to 5 mg/L, whatever dose was given.

question.stem: A drug is described as disposition rate limiting. What does that say about its two half-lives?

options.t: The absorption half-life is much the shorter of the two
options.why: Disposition rate limiting means the slow step is the drug's disposition, its elimination, rather than its arrival. For elimination to be the slow step, the absorption half-life must be the shorter, so ka is much larger than k. This is the ordinary situation for an oral product.

options.t: The absorption half-life is much longer than the elimination half-life
options.why: That is the definition of absorption rate limiting, the other of the two terms. The name tells you which process is the slow one, and the slow process is the one with the longer half-life. Swapping the two definitions is the whole risk in this pair.

Picking this avoids choosing between the two terms. Neither describes equal half-lives: disposition rate limiting means the absorption half-life is much the shorter, absorption rate limiting that it is much the longer. Equal constants would also leave the standard oral equation undefined, since ka − k in its denominator would be zero.

options.t: The elimination half-life cannot be determined from the absorption one
options.why: This reads a naming convention as a claim about what can be measured. The terms only say which process is slower. The elimination half-life is 0.693 divided by k in either case, and under disposition rate limiting it is the longer one and governs the tail of the curve.

list: Each term names the process that is rate limiting, meaning the slower one, for what is seen in the plasma; the longer half-life always belongs to it.
Disposition means everything that happens to a drug after it is absorbed, distribution and elimination together, so disposition rate limiting means elimination is the slow step.
Absorption rate limiting is the reverse.
Her slide "Absorption Kinetics Terminology" defines both terms by comparing the two half-lives.

question.quote: Disposition Rate Limiting: absorption half-life is much shorter than elimination half-life

question.stem: A female patient (35 years old, 65 kg) with normal renal function is to be given a drug by IV infusion. According to the literature, the elimination half-life of this drug is 7 hours and the apparent VD is 23.1% of body weight. The pharmacokinetics of this drug assumes a first-order process. The desired steady-state plasma level for this antibiotic is 10 mcg/mL. If the patient suddenly develops partial renal failure, how long would it take for a new steady-state plasma level to be established (assume that 95% of the Css is a reasonable approximation)?

options.why: 95% of Css takes 4.32 half-lives: 0.95 = 1 − e^(−kt) gives t = {{frac:ln 20|k}}. Renal failure lowers clearance and so lengthens the half-life, so the new half-life has to be found first, as her key says.

options.t: About 30.3 hours, as before the renal failure
options.why: Picking this keeps the old half-life. 30.3 hours is 4.32 half-lives of 7 hours; with less clearance k is smaller, the half-life is longer, and the new plateau is reached later.
This counts the right number of half-lives with the wrong half-life. After renal failure k = {{frac:ClT|VD}} falls, so each half-life is longer than 7 hours.

options.t: No time: the level stays at the old steady state
options.why: Picking this treats the plateau as fixed once reached. Css = {{frac:R|ClT}}; when ClT falls at the same rate R, the level rises toward a new, higher plateau, and that climb takes 4.32 of the new half-lives.

teach.h: A change in clearance during an infusion
list: Css = {{frac:R|ClT}}: lower clearance at the same rate gives a higher plateau.
k = {{frac:ClT|VD}}: lower clearance gives a smaller k and a longer half-life.
The time to the new plateau is set by the new half-life: 3 to 5 half-lives, or 4.32 for 95%.

question.quote: One would have to establish the new t½ for the patient, but the time to reach Css would be 4.32 t½ (see part a)
